procedural_history.originating_court: Magistrate Court (implied, based on police custody request)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Final Judgment and Order dated 08.10.2018 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Bench at Aurangabad in Criminal Writ Petition No.215 of 2017.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed Criminal Writ Petition No. 215 of 2017 in the High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Bench at Aurangabad on 02.02.2017, seeking initiation of departmental inquiry and criminal proceedings against respondent no.2, and also sought compensation. The High Court partly allowed the writ petition, awarding Rs. 75,000 to the appellant payable by respondent no.2 from his own pocket, but declined to direct initiation of criminal action under the SC/ST Act.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court by way of a Criminal Appeal (No. 1717 of 2024) challenging the High Court's Judgment and Order dated 08.10.2018, specifically likely challenging the part of the order that declined to direct initiation of criminal action under the SC/ST Act.

directions: The appeal stands disposed of by upholding the Impugned Judgment, with the modification that the respondent no.2 is held liable to pay a further sum of Rs.1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh only) to the appellant.
As the same stands already complied with, no further steps are required to be taken by the respondent no.2.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant is entitled to enhanced compensation for the violation of his fundamental right to personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution due to illegal detention by the police.

facts: The appellant was verbally and physically assaulted and illegally detained for four hours by a police officer (Respondent No. 2), even after being granted bail.
An internal police inquiry found Respondent No. 2 responsible for the excesses, but he only received a "strict warning" in departmental proceedings.
The High Court ordered Respondent No. 2 to pay Rs. 75,000 in compensation but declined to initiate criminal proceedings.
During the Supreme Court proceedings, Respondent No. 2 paid an additional Rs. 1,00,000 to the appellant, which the appellant accepted. The officer has also since retired (superannuated).
law: The High Court has the power under Article 226 of the Constitution to award compensation for the violation of fundamental rights.
Courts must take a zero-tolerance approach to police excesses and high-handed actions by those in positions of power.
Police forces are required to adhere to all established guidelines regarding arrest and the treatment of individuals in police custody.
application: The Supreme Court first affirmed that Respondent No. 2 had undoubtedly committed excesses and abused his official position, strongly denouncing his high-handed actions.
However, the Court balanced this finding against several other factors to decide on the appropriate remedy.
It noted that the officer had since retired from service.

Crucially, the Court considered the fact that the officer had already paid an additional Rs. 1,00,000 to the appellant (beyond what the High Court ordered) and that the appellant had accepted this payment.
The Court viewed this additional payment, which the appellant accepted, as a sufficient resolution to the claim for enhanced compensation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided to close the matter without ordering any further compensation or initiating criminal proceedings. It reasoned that although the officer's actions were a clear violation of the appellant's rights, the appellant had already received substantial additional compensation (Rs. 1,00,000) from the officer during the proceedings. Since the appellant accepted this payment and the officer had retired, the Court found it appropriate to give the matter a "quietus" (a final resolution), thus only partly satisfying the appellant's appeal for a formal enhancement order.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant is entitled to enhanced compensation for the violation of his fundamental right to personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution due to illegal detention by the police.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument, implicit in the appeal for enhanced compensation, is that his fundamental right to personal liberty under Article 21 was violated due to illegal detention by the police, and the compensation awarded or offered was insufficient.
respondent_arguments: The State (respondent) submitted that it had already initiated departmental proceedings against the police officer involved (respondent no. 2) and had awarded punishment.
Respondent no. 2 argued that the appellant's claim was entirely false, lodged by a habitual offender with the intent to demoralize the police.
Despite denying the claim, respondent no. 2 offered to pay the appellant a further compensation of Rs. 1,00,000.

cases.case_name: D K Basu v. State of West Bengal
cases.principle: For the court's power to issue directions and guidelines regarding arrest and police custody to prevent abuse of power.

cases.case_name: Sube Singh v. State of Haryana
cases.principle: For the court's power to award compensation for illegal detention and police excesses, and the need for police to adhere to guidelines.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Courts must adopt a zero-tolerance approach and take a very strict view of high-handed acts committed by persons in power against ordinary citizens.
obiter: The Supreme Court may refrain from initiating criminal proceedings under Article 142 of the Constitution against an official based on peculiar facts and circumstances, such as the official's retirement and payment of compensation, noting that justice ought to be tempered with mercy.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court refrained from directing the initiation of criminal proceedings against the retired police officer (respondent no. 2) under Article 142 of the Constitution, despite finding his actions to be high-handed. This decision was made due to the "peculiar facts and circumstances" of the case, specifically that the officer had retired and had already paid a total compensation of Rs. 1,75,000 to the appellant, leading the court to conclude that justice ought to be tempered with mercy.
legal_tests_applied: The court considered exercising its power under Article 142 of the Constitution to direct the initiation of criminal proceedings but ultimately decided against it by balancing the severity of the act against mitigating factors.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant did not succeed in having criminal proceedings initiated against the police officer because the court chose to refrain from such a direction based on a combination of factors: the officer had already retired, he had paid a total of Rs. 1,75,000 in compensation, and the court's view that justice should be tempered with mercy in these specific circumstances.
why_respondent_won: The respondent officer (no. 2) avoided the initiation of criminal proceedings because he had retired and had already paid a substantial amount of compensation (Rs. 1,75,000 in total), which led the court to exercise restraint and apply the principle of mercy.
policy_considerations: Courts need to take a very strict view and adopt a zero-tolerance approach towards high-handed acts committed by persons in power against ordinary citizens, as such acts bring shame to the entire justice delivery system.
In peculiar facts and circumstances, justice ought to be tempered with mercy.
